title: Google’s top hacker hunter explains why hacking groups get codenames
slides: Who names hacking groups, and why does it matter?
Google's top hunter says codenames often reveal attacker origins.
But many names are wrong—researchers misattribute them constantly.
You may be hunting the wrong group because of a bad codename.
Verify attacker identity yourself; never trust the label blindly.
thread_text:
1. Who names the hackers?

Google's top hunter says codenames often reveal where attackers come from, but the labels are frequently wrong.

2. The mislabeling problem

Researchers constantly misattribute groups. A bad codename can send you chasing the wrong threat.

3. Why labels fail

Names are chosen for effect, not accuracy. Political and marketing pressures skew what you see.

4. Chase the real target

If the label is wrong, your defense strategy may be completely off. Identify the attacker by behavior, not name.

5. Verify before you act

Next time you see a group name, run your own data analysis. Never trust the label blindly—test it yourself.
video_script: Labels reveal origins, but often wrong.
Misattribution sends you hunting false targets.
Verify identity yourself with your data.
Don't trust the name, trust the evidence.

instagram.caption:
A hacking group's codename might be completely wrong—and that's not a small detail.

Google's top threat hunter says researchers constantly misattribute attacks to the wrong groups. The codenames you see in reports are chosen for effect, not accuracy, and political or marketing pressure can skew what gets published.

If you're chasing a label instead of behavior, your defense strategy might be aimed at the wrong threat entirely. A bad name literally redirects your security work to a dead end.

Before you act on any group attribution, run your own data analysis. Don't let a catchy codename decide where you spend your attention 🎯🕵️

When was the last time you verified a threat group's identity yourself?🔍
